stages.title: Observational drawing
stages.hook: Draw your hand for one minute without looking at the paper. What did you notice about what you really see?
explain: Observational drawing means drawing what you actually see, not what you think something looks like. Beginners often draw symbols, such as a flat round eye, because the brain stores simple ideas. Careful looking replaces those symbols with real shapes, angles and proportions.

Useful tools help. Sighting uses a pencil held at arm's length to measure one part against another. Negative space means drawing the shapes between and around objects, which often feels easier than drawing the object itself. Blind contour drawing, where you follow the edge slowly without looking at the paper, trains hand and eye together.

Check angles by comparing a line with a vertical or horizontal reference. Step back from the drawing to compare it with the subject. Artists in every tradition train through close study, from Chinese brush masters copying nature to students in West African and European workshops.

example.q: A bottle appears 20 cm tall and 5 cm wide in your sight-size measurement. How many widths tall is it?
steps: The bottle is four widths tall.

analogies.home: Drawing the gap between chair legs is negative space.
analogies.sport: A coach compares one player's height against the goalpost to judge scale, like sighting.
analogies.nature: Drawing the sky shapes between branches shows the tree.
analogies.tech: Zooming into a photo to compare distances works like comparative measuring.

stages.mnemonic: See the shape, not the name; measure twice, then draw.
terms: Measuring proportions by comparing parts against a unit with a held pencil.
The empty shape around and between objects.
Drawing an edge slowly without looking at the paper.
Drawing what we know instead of what we see.

misc.wrong: Good drawing depends on talent more than looking.
misc.right: Observation can be trained. Measuring and comparing help anyone draw more accurately.

stages.limits: Sighting works best from one fixed viewpoint, which is not always possible with a moving subject.

stages.title: Human figure drawing
stages.hook: Strike a pose and hold it for ten seconds. Where do you feel your weight, and how would you draw that?
explain: Figure drawing studies the human body to understand proportion, balance and movement. It is about shapes and gesture, not details. Artists start with a quick gesture line that catches the main movement of the pose.

Then the body is simplified into basic forms: an oval for the head, a box for the chest, a box for the hips, and cylinders for limbs. The body is often measured in heads. Many guides use about 7.5 to 8 heads for an adult, and the halfway point of the body falls near the hips. This is a guideline because real bodies vary.

Artists check balance by imagining a vertical line from the pit of the neck to the ground. If the figure stands on one leg, that line falls near the supporting foot. Ancient Egyptian artists used grids of squares for consistent proportion. Sculptors in Benin, Greece and India each developed their own ideal proportions, which show how cultures shape what a body should look like.

example.q: A figure is 8 heads tall and each head is 3 cm. How tall is the drawing?

analogies.sport: A sprinter's gesture line shows lean, push and stretch before any muscles are drawn.
analogies.home: A mannequin or wooden artist's doll shows how the body is built from simple parts.
analogies.music: A dancer holds a balanced pose just as a note holds steady.
analogies.tech: Animators use rough stick figures to plan movement before final drawings.

stages.mnemonic: Gesture first, forms next, hang the weight on a line.
terms: The flow of movement in a pose.
The size relationships between body parts.
A simple model built from ovals, boxes and cylinders.
An imagined vertical line showing where weight is supported.

misc.wrong: A figure must always be exactly eight heads tall.
misc.right: Eight heads is a convenient guideline. Real people vary, and artists change proportion on purpose.

stages.limits: Idealised proportion systems reflect cultural preferences and are not universal truths.

stages.title: Portraiture
stages.hook: Look at a face. Where are the eyes: higher, lower, or halfway down the head? Check before you answer.
explain: A portrait shows a particular person. It can capture appearance, but also character and place in the world. Some portraits are formal, some are playful, and a self-portrait is an artist drawing or painting themselves.

A face has helpful proportions. In a front view, the eyes sit about halfway down the head, with the bottom of the nose roughly halfway between the eyes and the chin and the mouth about a third of the way from nose to chin. The distance between the eyes is about one eye width. Faces vary, so these are starting guides, not rules.

Portraits appear in every culture. The Fayum mummy portraits were painted in Roman-period Egypt in the first to third centuries CE. Ife heads from Nigeria show careful naturalistic faces. Rembrandt made many self-portraits in the 1600s, and Frida Kahlo painted herself in the 1900s. Many Mughal court portraits in South Asia were painted in fine detail.

example.q: A head is 20 cm tall in a front view. About how far from the top of the head are the eyes?
steps: Use the guide: eyes are about halfway down.

analogies.home: A school photo is a kind of portrait, but a painted portrait may show personality too.
analogies.city: Statues in public squares often portray important people.
analogies.sport: A medal photo shows pride, not just a face.
analogies.music: Album covers often use portraits to show an artist's character.

stages.mnemonic: Eyes are halfway, nose in the middle, mouth just above the chin's third.
terms: An artwork showing a particular person.
How closely a portrait resembles the sitter.

misc.wrong: A portrait only needs to copy the face.
misc.right: Portraits can also show personality, status, mood and story through pose, clothes and setting.

stages.limits: Facial proportion rules are averages. Individual faces differ, and some artists distort on purpose.

stages.title: Landscape painting
stages.hook: Why do far mountains look blue and pale, while near trees look dark and sharp?
explain: A landscape shows natural or built scenery. Painters organise landscapes into foreground, middle ground and background. The foreground has most detail and strongest colour. The background is simpler.

This effect is atmospheric perspective. Air, dust and moisture make distant things lighter, bluer and less sharp. Painters imitate it by mixing a little blue-grey and white into far hills and softening edges. Linear perspective also helps, with paths and fields narrowing toward a vanishing point.

Landscape has strong traditions everywhere. Chinese shan shui, meaning mountain-water, painting shows misty mountains on scrolls. Katsushika Hokusai and Utagawa Hiroshige made landscape woodblock prints in nineteenth-century Japan. Albert Namatjira, a Western Aranda artist, painted watercolour landscapes of Central Australia from the 1930s. Claude Monet painted outdoors in France in the later 1800s.

example.q: A far blue ridge, a middle field and a near tree. Which should be palest and softest?
steps: The furthest layer is palest and bluest.
So the blue ridge is the palest.

stages.title: Still-life painting
stages.hook: Arrange three objects on a table and light them from one side. What story do they seem to tell?
explain: A still life shows objects that do not move, such as fruit, bottles, flowers or tools. Artists choose and arrange the objects, so it is a study of composition, light, colour and texture.

Good still lifes use a clear light direction, overlapping shapes, contrast of sizes and a path for the eye. Reflections and different surfaces, such as shiny metal beside a rough cloth, make practice in showing texture.

Still life has a long history. Roman wall paintings and mosaics from Pompeii show food and glassware. In the 1600s, Dutch artists painted lavish tables and "vanitas" pictures with symbols of time passing. Paul Cézanne painted apples to study shape and colour in the late 1800s. Chinese flower-and-bird painting and Mexican painted ceramics also celebrate everyday objects.

example.q: Light shines from the left on an apple. Where is the darkest side and the cast shadow?
steps: The side facing away is darkest: the right side.
The cast shadow falls on the table to the right.
Reflected light may lift the edge.
example.a: The right side is darkest and the shadow falls to the right

stages.title: Perspective construction
stages.hook: Look at the corner of a building. Why do both walls seem to slope toward the horizon?
explain: In two-point perspective, a box is seen from a corner. Vertical edges stay vertical. The horizontal edges slope toward two vanishing points on the horizon line, one left and one right.

To construct a box, draw the horizon line. Place two vanishing points far apart on it. Draw the near vertical edge. From its top and bottom, draw lines to each vanishing point. Add the far vertical edges, then join the new corners back to the vanishing points to finish the top and base.

Circles seen in perspective become ellipses. Foreshortening makes an object pointing toward you look short. Linear perspective developed in Europe in the 1400s, and similar tools are used in architecture and film today. Other traditions show space with isometric, stacked or multiple viewpoints, which are not wrong, just different.

example.q: A horizon line has two vanishing points. How many sets of receding horizontal edges does a box have?
steps: Edges of the left face go to VP1.
Edges of the right face go to VP2.
So there are two sets of receding horizontals.

stages.title: Clay and ceramic sculpture
stages.hook: Why do pots need to dry slowly before they go in a kiln? What could go wrong if the clay is still damp?
explain: Ceramics is shaping clay and making it hard by firing. Hand-building methods are pinch, coil and slab. The potter's wheel shapes round forms by spinning. Before shaping, clay is wedged, which means kneaded to remove air bubbles and make it even.

Clay goes through stages. Wet clay is soft. Leather-hard clay is firm enough to carve and join. Bone-dry clay is fully dry and fragile. Bisque firing, often around 900 to 1000 degrees Celsius, makes it hard but porous. A glaze, a glassy coating, is then applied and fired again, often at higher temperatures. Clay shrinks as it dries and fires.

If damp clay is fired, trapped water turns to steam and can crack or burst the piece. Pottery appears worldwide: Jōmon pots in Japan are over 10,000 years old, Nok terracotta figures from Nigeria are over 2,000 years old, and Pueblo potters in North America have long made decorated vessels. Always have a trained adult operate a kiln.

stages.title: Wood and stone sculpture appreciation
stages.hook: How do you think someone carved a huge figure from one block, and how would you look at it with respect?
explain: Carving removes material to reveal a form. Wood has a grain, and carvers usually cut along or across it with sharp gouges and chisels. Stone is cut with chisels and hammers, then smoothed with abrasives. Hard stones like granite last long. Softer stones like soapstone are easier to carve.

Appreciating sculpture means walking around it, looking at material, scale, surface and purpose. Ask: who made it, for whom, and what does it do? Some works are sacred or belong to living communities, so we look with respect.

Great Zimbabwe, in southern Africa, has soapstone bird sculptures from the 1200s to 1400s. Haida and other Indigenous nations of the Pacific Northwest of North America carve totem poles from cedar to record family histories. Khmer builders carved relief stories at Angkor in Cambodia. The Moai on Rapa Nui were carved from volcanic rock. Michelangelo carved his marble works in Italy around 1500.

example.q: A carver wants a thin projecting arm on a wooden figure. Should the arm run along the grain or across it?
steps: Wood splits easily along its grain.
A thin part running across the grain has short fibres to hold it.
So the arm should run along the grain.
example.a: Along the grain, where the fibres are long and strong

stages.title: Visual storytelling
stages.hook: Tell a whole story with no words: what is the smallest number of pictures you need?
explain: Visual storytelling uses images in order to tell a story. A single picture can hint at a story, and a series of pictures can show change over time. Artists choose what to show, from what angle, and what to leave out.

Tools include sequence, framing (close-up, medium, wide), colour, and showing cause and effect. In comics, panels are the boxes, the gutter is the space between them, and the reader's mind fills in what happens in the gap. Manga is traditionally read from right to left.

People have told stories in images for thousands of years. Egyptian tomb reliefs show daily life in rows. The Bayeux Tapestry, an embroidered cloth about 70 metres long, tells the story of events in 1066. Mexican screenfold codices recorded histories and calendars. Warli paintings in India show daily life with simple shapes. Every culture's way of ordering a story is valid.

steps: Look at the order: seed first.
